metadata.title: Kotlin & Android Engineering Curriculum
metadata.description: Comprehensive foundation for modern Kotlin, Android, and Clean Architecture engineering.

topics.name: Kotlin Fundamentals
topics.description: Master core Kotlin programming, modern language syntax, and coroutines.

topics.name: Android Fundamentals
topics.description: Build robust Android applications with Jetpack Compose, Lifecycle, and Room.

topics.name: Architecture & Engineering
topics.description: Design modular, maintainable, and testable applications using Clean Architecture.

cards.title: Kotlin Basic Syntax
cards.summary: Kotlin is a modern, statically typed programming language that compiles to Java bytecode.
cards.whyItMatters: It is the official and preferred language for modern Android development.
cards.realWorldExample: Google uses Kotlin for Android APIs and internal tooling.
cards.commonMistakes: Confusing val (read-only) with var (mutable).
cards.whenNotToUse: Low-level system programming where JVM overhead is unacceptable.
cards.bestPractice: Use val (immutable) variables by default unless mutability is required.

cards.title: Variables and Immutability
cards.summary: Kotlin separates read-only references (val) from mutable variables (var).
cards.whyItMatters: Immutability eliminates side-effects, race conditions, and accidental state modification.
cards.realWorldExample: Declaring configuration parameters, domain models, and UI state as val.
cards.commonMistakes: Defaulting to var out of habit from other languages.
cards.whenNotToUse: Local loop counters or performance-sensitive internal mutable accumulators.
cards.bestPractice: Always declare references with val; change to var only when reassignment is strictly needed.

cards.title: Null Safety & Nullable Types
cards.summary: Kotlin's type system distinguishes nullable types (Type?) from non-nullable types (Type).
cards.whyItMatters: Eliminates NullPointerException (The Billion Dollar Mistake) at compile-time.
cards.realWorldExample: Handling optional network response fields without crashing.
cards.commonMistakes: Overusing the double-bang (!!) operator instead of safe calls (?.) or Elvis (?:).
cards.whenNotToUse: Forcing non-null assertion (!!) on values that could be null under network failure.
cards.bestPractice: Use safe call operators (?.) and the Elvis operator (?:) to supply sensible fallback defaults.

cards.title: Functions & Default Arguments
cards.summary: Kotlin functions support named arguments, default parameter values, and single-expression syntax.
cards.whyItMatters: Drastically reduces the need for overloaded constructor and method boilerplate.
cards.realWorldExample: Creating API client methods with optional timeout and retry parameters.
cards.commonMistakes: Creating dozens of overloaded methods in Kotlin instead of leveraging default parameters.
cards.whenNotToUse: When interacting with legacy Java code without @JvmOverloads annotations.
cards.bestPractice: Use single-expression functions for simple one-line transformations.

cards.title: Collections: List, Set, and Map
cards.summary: Kotlin distinguishes read-only collection interfaces (List) from mutable counterparts (MutableList).
cards.whyItMatters: Protects data integrity by exposing unmodifiable views of collections from repositories and ViewModels.
cards.realWorldExample: Exposing StateFlow<List<Item>> to the UI while keeping MutableStateFlow private.
cards.commonMistakes: Casting List to MutableList instead of creating a defensive copy.
cards.whenNotToUse: Exposing mutable collections directly across architectural boundaries.
cards.bestPractice: Always return read-only collection interfaces from public functions and classes.

cards.title: Data Classes & Value Immutability
cards.summary: Data classes automatically generate equals(), hashCode(), toString(), componentN(), and copy() functions.
cards.whyItMatters: Simplifies creating immutable Value Objects, DTOs, and UI state wrappers.
cards.realWorldExample: Representing UserProfile, PaymentIntent, or ScreenState models.
cards.commonMistakes: Creating mutable properties (var) inside data classes.
cards.whenNotToUse: Entities with mutable internal state or complex inheritance hierarchies.
cards.bestPractice: Make all data class constructor properties val and use copy() for immutable modifications.

cards.title: Sealed Classes & Exhaustive State Modeling
cards.summary: Sealed classes represent restricted class hierarchies where all subclasses are known at compile time.
cards.whyItMatters: Enables exhaustive when expressions without requiring error-prone else branches.
cards.realWorldExample: Modeling UI states: Sealed interface UiState { Loading, Success, Error }.
cards.commonMistakes: Adding a default 'else' branch in when expressions, bypassing compile-time safety on new state additions.
cards.whenNotToUse: Open polymorphism where third-party modules need to extend subclasses dynamically.
cards.bestPractice: Use sealed interfaces for modeling domain events, UI states, and operation outcomes.

cards.title: Extension Functions
cards.summary: Extension functions extend a class with new functionality without inheriting or modifying the original class.
cards.whyItMatters: Provides readable, fluent API utilities without cluttering utility helper classes.
cards.realWorldExample: Converting domain models to UI view models: fun User.toUiState(): UserUiState.
cards.commonMistakes: Overusing extension functions on standard types (like String/Int) with ambiguous names.
cards.whenNotToUse: Accessing private or protected members of the receiver class.
cards.bestPractice: Keep extensions domain-scoped and place them in cohesive, top-level files.

cards.title: Coroutines & Structured Concurrency
cards.summary: Coroutines provide lightweight, non-blocking asynchronous execution managed by scopes and dispatchers.
cards.whyItMatters: Prevents ANR (Application Not Responding) crashes by offloading expensive work from the Main thread.
cards.realWorldExample: Performing database queries and network calls with suspend functions.
cards.commonMistakes: Launching unconfined coroutines with GlobalScope instead of viewModelScope / lifecycleScope.
cards.whenNotToUse: Blocking CPU-bound tasks without switching to Dispatchers.Default.
cards.bestPractice: Always adhere to structured concurrency by tying coroutine lifecycles to component scopes.

cards.title: Kotlin Flow & Reactive Streams
cards.summary: Flow is a cold asynchronous stream that emits values sequentially according to reactive stream principles.
cards.whyItMatters: Allows reactive data propagation from Room/Network layers all the way to Compose UI.
cards.realWorldExample: Streaming real-time database query results to UI state collectors.
cards.commonMistakes: Collecting cold Flows directly in Compose without repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle.
cards.whenNotToUse: Single one-shot requests where a simple suspend function is clearer.
cards.bestPractice: Use StateFlow for state holding and SharedFlow for one-time navigation/toast events.

cards.title: Activity & Single-Activity Architecture
cards.summary: An Activity is an entry point for user interaction, serving as the host window in modern Android apps.
cards.whyItMatters: Modern Android development uses a Single-Activity Architecture hosting Jetpack Compose screens.
cards.realWorldExample: MainActivity acting as the root entry point that sets the Compose content.
cards.commonMistakes: Placing business logic, database calls, or state management inside Activity classes.
cards.whenNotToUse: Creating multiple heavyweight Activities for every individual screen.
cards.bestPractice: Keep Activity lightweight: initialize Hilt, theme, and host root Compose Navigation.

cards.title: Android Lifecycle & State Management
cards.summary: Lifecycle-aware components respond to system lifecycle state transitions (CREATED, STARTED, RESUMED, DESTROYED).
cards.whyItMatters: Prevents memory leaks, crashes during backgrounding, and unnecessary battery consumption.
cards.realWorldExample: Pausing camera preview or location tracking in onStop() and resuming in onStart().
cards.commonMistakes: Updating UI components after the view is destroyed.
cards.whenNotToUse: Relying on Activity destruction for normal state clearing.
cards.bestPractice: Use LifecycleObserver and lifecycle-aware coroutine scopes to bind background tasks safely.

cards.title: ViewModel & Configuration Changes
cards.summary: ViewModel stores and manages UI-related data in a lifecycle-conscious way that survives screen rotations.
cards.whyItMatters: Eliminates data loss during screen rotation and configuration changes.
cards.realWorldExample: Maintaining search query results and form inputs when user rotates their phone.
cards.commonMistakes: Holding references to Context, Activity, or View inside a ViewModel (causing memory leaks).
cards.whenNotToUse: Storing persistent disk data that must survive process death (use Room or SavedStateHandle).
cards.bestPractice: Expose UI state as StateFlow and handle user actions through clear ViewModel methods.

cards.title: Jetpack Compose Declarative UI
cards.summary: Jetpack Compose is Android's modern toolkit for building native UI using declarative Kotlin functions.
cards.whyItMatters: Simplifies and accelerates UI development by eliminating XML layout and view-binding boilerplate.
cards.realWorldExample: Creating responsive list layouts using LazyColumn and Card composables.
cards.commonMistakes: Performing heavy calculations or side-effects directly inside composable functions.
cards.whenNotToUse: Triggering network calls inside a Composable without LaunchedEffect.
cards.bestPractice: Keep composable functions pure and stateless by passing data down and events up.

cards.title: State Hoisting in Jetpack Compose
cards.summary: State hoisting is a pattern of moving state to a caller to make a composable stateless, reusable, and testable.
cards.whyItMatters: Stateless composables are easy to preview, unit test, and reuse across multiple screens.
cards.realWorldExample: TextField receiving value: String and onValueChange: (String) -> Unit from parent screen.
cards.commonMistakes: Hardcoding ViewModel calls inside deep leaf composables.
cards.whenNotToUse: Ephemeral animations that belong entirely to a single self-contained UI widget.
cards.bestPractice: Pass explicit state objects into composables and propagate interactions via event lambdas.

cards.title: Room Local Persistence
cards.summary: Room provides an abstraction layer over SQLite to allow fluent database access while leveraging compile-time SQL verification.
cards.whyItMatters: Guarantees compile-time safety for database queries and native coroutines/Flow integration.
cards.realWorldExample: Storing user profiles, offline learning packages, and cognitive memory records.
cards.commonMistakes: Executing database operations on the main thread (causing crashes).
cards.whenNotToUse: Storing simple key-value settings (use Jetpack DataStore instead).
cards.bestPractice: Define DAOs with suspend functions and return Flow<T> for reactive data streams.

cards.title: Dependency Injection with Hilt
cards.summary: Hilt is Android's standard dependency injection library built on top of Dagger to provide compile-time DI.
cards.whyItMatters: Decouples object creation from business logic, making code modular, maintainable, and easily mockable in tests.
cards.realWorldExample: Injecting repositories and domain use cases into ViewModels with @Inject constructor.
cards.commonMistakes: Creating manual singletons with static global variables instead of Hilt @Singleton components.
cards.whenNotToUse: Injecting framework Android components into pure domain models.
cards.bestPractice: Bind repository interfaces to implementations using @Binds within clean Hilt modules.

cards.title: Clean Architecture Layer Isolation
cards.summary: Clean Architecture separates concerns into Presentation, Domain, and Data layers with strict inward dependency rules.
cards.whyItMatters: Core business logic remains completely independent of UI frameworks, databases, and third-party libraries.
cards.realWorldExample: Structuring an Android app with core:domain, core:storage, and feature modules.
cards.commonMistakes: Allowing domain layer entities to import Android SDK or Room database classes.
cards.whenNotToUse: Trivial one-screen utility scripts with zero business rules.
cards.bestPractice: Domain layer must contain only pure Kotlin code, business use cases, and repository interfaces.

cards.title: Repository Pattern & Single Source of Truth
cards.summary: The Repository pattern mediates between domain logic and data sources (local database, remote network API).
cards.whyItMatters: Provides a clean API for data access while encapsulating caching, network synchronization, and offline fallback.
cards.realWorldExample: KnowledgePackageRepository fetching from Room and synchronizing with remote updates.
cards.commonMistakes: Exposing raw Room Database Entities directly to ViewModels and UI Composables.
cards.whenNotToUse: Accessing hardware sensor streams directly from UI components without abstraction.
cards.bestPractice: Map data transfer entities to pure domain models inside the repository layer.

cards.title: Use Cases & Domain Workflows
cards.summary: Use Cases (interactors) encapsulate single, reusable units of business logic in the domain layer.
cards.whyItMatters: Prevents fat ViewModels and enables straightforward testing of business workflows.
cards.realWorldExample: InitializeApplicationWorkflow, FinishReviewWorkflow, and BuildDailyFeedWorkflow.
cards.commonMistakes: Creating pass-through use cases that merely call repository without adding business logic.
cards.whenNotToUse: Direct UI formatting or presentation-specific transformations.
cards.bestPractice: Every use case should have a single public execute() or invoke() operator function.

cards.title: SOLID Principles in Kotlin
cards.summary: SOLID is an acronym for five design principles that make software designs understandable, flexible, and maintainable.
cards.whyItMatters: Protects codebases from architectural decay as feature complexity and team size grow.
cards.realWorldExample: Using Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion to mock repositories in unit tests.
cards.commonMistakes: Violating Single Responsibility by stuffing business rules, network calls, and UI handlers into one class.
cards.whenNotToUse: Over-engineering simple one-off data scripts with dozens of unused interfaces.
cards.bestPractice: Depend on abstractions (interfaces) rather than concrete implementations.

cards.title: Multi-Module Android Architecture
cards.summary: Modularization divides a monolithic application codebase into loosely coupled, independent Gradle subprojects.
cards.whyItMatters: Improves build speed with parallel compilation, enforces architectural boundaries, and enables code reuse.
cards.realWorldExample: Separating app into :core:domain, :core:storage, :core:ui, and feature modules.
cards.commonMistakes: Creating circular dependencies between feature modules.
cards.whenNotToUse: Small prototype apps where multi-module overhead outweighs build benefits.
cards.bestPractice: Features should depend on shared core APIs, never directly on other feature implementation modules.

cards.title: Unit Testing with JUnit & MockK
cards.summary: Unit tests verify that individual units of source code function correctly in complete isolation from external frameworks.
cards.whyItMatters: Enables rapid refactoring, catches regressions instantly, and acts as living code documentation.
cards.realWorldExample: Testing InitializeApplicationWorkflow with deterministic fake repository doubles.
cards.commonMistakes: Writing brittle tests that test internal private implementation details instead of public behavior.
cards.whenNotToUse: Testing Android framework drawing and rendering (use UI screenshot testing instead).
cards.bestPractice: Follow Arrange-Act-Assert structure and use deterministic Dispatchers in coroutine tests.

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used to declare a read-only variable in Kotlin?

options.text: val
options.explanation: Correct. val declares a read-only local variable.

options.text: var
options.explanation: Incorrect. var declares a mutable variable.

questions.questionText: Can a variable declared with val be reassigned after initialization?

options.text: No, val references are immutable once assigned
options.explanation: Correct. val cannot be reassigned after initialization.

options.text: Yes, if it is inside a function
options.explanation: Incorrect. val cannot be reassigned regardless of scope.

questions.questionText: Which operator safely calls a method only if the target reference is non-null?

options.explanation: Correct. The safe call operator (?.) returns null if receiver is null.
Incorrect. !! throws NullPointerException if the receiver is null.

questions.questionText: What feature in Kotlin avoids creating multiple overloaded methods?

options.text: Default parameter values
options.explanation: Correct. Default arguments allow callers to omit optional arguments.

options.text: Dynamic typing
options.explanation: Incorrect. Kotlin is statically typed.

questions.questionText: Is the standard Kotlin List<T> interface mutable by default?

options.text: No, List<T> is read-only; use MutableList<T> for mutation
options.explanation: Correct. List<T> does not expose mutating methods like add() or remove().

options.text: Yes, all Kotlin collections are mutable
options.explanation: Incorrect. Kotlin separates read-only and mutable collection interfaces.

questions.questionText: Which generated method allows creating modified immutable copies of a data class?

options.text: copy()
options.explanation: Correct. copy() creates a shallow clone with selectively updated fields.

options.text: clone()
options.explanation: Incorrect. Kotlin data classes provide copy().

questions.questionText: Why do sealed classes enable exhaustive when expressions without an else branch?

options.text: The compiler knows all permitted subclasses at compile-time
options.explanation: Correct. Sealed hierarchies are closed and fully verifiable by the compiler.

options.text: Sealed classes automatically implement Java Enums
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sealed classes allow subclasses with distinct state.

questions.questionText: How are Kotlin extension functions resolved under the hood?

options.text: Statically based on the declared receiver type
options.explanation: Correct. Extension functions are compiled as static methods.

options.text: Dynamically using runtime reflection and byte-weaving
options.explanation: Incorrect. Extensions are statically dispatched with zero reflection overhead.

questions.questionText: Does calling a suspend function block the underlying thread?

options.text: No, it suspends execution without blocking the underlying thread
options.explanation: Correct. Suspension frees the underlying thread to execute other tasks.

options.text: Yes, it puts the thread into a Thread.sleep state
options.explanation: Incorrect. Coroutines are non-blocking.

questions.questionText: By default, is a standard Kotlin Flow hot or cold?

options.text: Cold (does not produce values until collected)
options.explanation: Correct. Flow blocks only start emitting when a collector begins.

options.text: Hot (emits values regardless of collectors)
options.explanation: Incorrect. StateFlow and SharedFlow are hot, but standard Flow is cold.

questions.questionText: In modern Jetpack Compose architecture, what is the role of MainActivity?

options.text: A lightweight entry point and window host for Compose screens
options.explanation: Correct. Single-Activity pattern hosts the root composable tree.

options.text: Holding all business logic and database connections
options.explanation: Incorrect. Business logic belongs in Domain Use Cases and ViewModels.

questions.questionText: Which lifecycle state indicates the app is in the foreground and interactive?

options.text: RESUMED
options.explanation: Correct. In RESUMED state, the activity is in the foreground and has focus.

options.text: STOPPED
options.explanation: Incorrect. STOPPED indicates the UI is no longer visible.

questions.questionText: Does a Jetpack ViewModel survive screen rotation?

options.text: Yes, it is retained across configuration changes
options.explanation: Correct. ViewModel is designed to retain UI state across configuration changes.

options.text: No, it is destroyed and recreated on every rotation
options.explanation: Incorrect. ViewModels survive configuration changes.

questions.questionText: What process updates the UI when Compose state changes?

options.text: Recomposition
options.explanation: Correct. Compose calls the composable functions again with new data.

options.text: DOM re-rendering
options.explanation: Incorrect. Recomposition is Jetpack Compose's update mechanism.

questions.questionText: In Compose state hoisting, what goes down and what goes up?

options.text: State goes down, events go up
options.explanation: Correct. Parameters pass state down, callbacks pass events up.

options.text: Events go down, state goes up
options.explanation: Incorrect. Unidirectional data flow passes state down and events up.

questions.questionText: When does Room verify SQL queries written in @Query annotations?

options.text: At compile time
options.explanation: Correct. Room validates SQL syntax and table columns during compilation.

options.text: Only at runtime when the query is first executed
options.explanation: Incorrect. Compile-time verification is a key feature of Room.

questions.questionText: Which annotation injects dependencies into an Android ViewModel using Hilt?

options.text: @HiltViewModel and @Inject constructor
options.explanation: Correct. @HiltViewModel marks the ViewModel for Hilt injection.

options.text: @AndroidEntryPoint only
options.explanation: Incorrect. @AndroidEntryPoint is for Activities, Fragments, and Views.

questions.questionText: According to Clean Architecture, can the Domain layer depend on the Data or UI layer?

options.text: No, dependencies must point inward toward the Domain layer
options.explanation: Correct. Domain is completely independent of external layers.

options.text: Yes, Domain can freely import Room DAOs and Composables
options.explanation: Incorrect. Violates Clean Architecture dependency rule.

questions.questionText: What is the primary responsibility of a Repository in Clean Architecture?

options.text: To abstract data sources and provide a single source of truth
options.explanation: Correct. Repositories mediate between domain workflows and storage/network.

options.text: To render UI elements and handle touch events
options.explanation: Incorrect. UI rendering belongs in the presentation layer.

questions.questionText: How many business workflows should a single Use Case class encapsulate?

options.text: Exactly one discrete business action (Single Responsibility)
options.explanation: Correct. Use cases represent atomic business operations.

options.text: All operations for an entire database table
options.explanation: Incorrect. That describes a DAO or Repository.

questions.questionText: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle (D in SOLID) state?

options.text: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete details
options.explanation: Correct. Both high and low level modules must depend on abstractions.

options.text: All classes must be declared as static singletons
options.explanation: Incorrect. Static singletons increase tight coupling.

questions.questionText: What is a major engineering benefit of modularizing an Android codebase?

options.text: Faster incremental builds and strict architectural encapsulation
options.explanation: Correct. Gradle can build independent modules in parallel.

options.text: Eliminating all unit testing requirements
options.explanation: Incorrect. Modularization makes unit testing even easier.

questions.questionText: Why are unit tests run on the local JVM instead of a real Android device?

options.text: For fast execution speed without emulator/device startup overhead
options.explanation: Correct. JVM unit tests execute in milliseconds.

options.text: Because Kotlin code cannot be executed on Android
options.explanation: Incorrect. Android runs Kotlin natively.
